title: Listen to 4+ Hours of Jazz & Classical Music from Haruki Murakami’s Novels
description: Before he became a nov­el­ist, Haru­ki Muraka­mi ran a jazz bar in Tokyo, and music has filled his nov­els ever since. For your lis­ten­ing p
body:
Before he became a nov­el­ist, Haru­ki Muraka­mi ran a jazz bar in Tokyo, and music has filled his nov­els ever since. For your lis­ten­ing plea­sure, NTS Radio has cre­at­ed two playlists of the jazz and clas­si­cal music ref­er­enced in his fic­tion. Togeth­er, they run near­ly five hours and fea­ture every­one from John Coltrane, Bill Evans, and Thelo­nious Monk to Schu­bert, Liszt, and Mozart. Our sug­ges­tion: Pick up a Muraka­mi nov­el, press play, and let the music become the sound­track to your read­ing. Enjoy!

title: When Galileo Calculated the Precise Dimensions of Hell in Dante’s Inferno
description:
in History, Literature, Religion, Science |   	September 21st, 2026  1 Comment
	
			
We ven­er­ate Galileo Galilei for dar­ing to speak the sci­en­t
body:
in History, Literature, Religion, Science |   	September 21st, 2026  1 Comment
	
			
We ven­er­ate Galileo Galilei for dar­ing to speak the sci­en­tif­ic truth in the face of severe insti­tu­tion­al oppo­si­tion. He pub­licly acknowl­edged that the Earth revolves around the Sun in a time when the Church would rather he did­n’t, dis­play­ing a bloody-mind­ed­ness that he seems to have acquired with age. Decades ear­li­er, in the first stage of his career, he found him­self (cir­ca 1588) tasked by the Flo­ren­tine Acad­e­my with cal­cu­lat­ing the pre­cise dimen­sions of hell as described in Dan­te’s Divine Com­e­dy. Duti­ful­ly apply­ing him­self to this now-absurd-sound­ing work, he deter­mined that the under­world’s roof had to be cen­tered in Jerusalem, as wide as the radius of the entire Earth, and no less than 600 kilo­me­ters thick.
Not that any of this was based on friv­o­lous rea­son­ing. As a mod­el for the dimen­sions of hel­l’s roof, for instance, Galileo looked over to Fil­ip­po Brunelleschi’s dome, which had topped the Flo­rence Cathe­dral for a cen­tu­ry and a half at that point. Galileo’s cal­cu­la­tions of hel­l’s dimen­sions con­tra­dict­ed an ear­li­er mod­el pro­posed by the schol­ar Alessan­dro Vel­lutel­lo. Instead, they sup­port­ed a mod­el devel­oped by archi­tect Anto­nio Manet­ti, whose draw­ings appear here.
That Manet­ti was a fel­low Flo­ren­tine, and Vel­lutel­lo was from Flo­rence’s long­time rival Luc­ca could well have count­ed among the moti­vat­ing fac­tors. But we must bear in mind that, in the six­teenth cen­tu­ry, peo­ple real­ly did want to get these facts straight — if “facts” be the prop­er term.

The attempt to rec­on­cile scrip­ture with objec­tiv­i­ty absorbed the lives of many high­ly intel­li­gent peo­ple through­out the Mid­dle Ages and the Renais­sance. How­ev­er hope­less that goal could be, the thought Galileo devot­ed to the prob­lem may have result­ed in a gen­uine break­through. Math­e­mati­cian and sci­ence his­to­ri­an Mark Peter­son, pre­vi­ous­ly fea­tured here on Open Cul­ture, has argued that his cal­cu­la­tions of Dan­te’s non-Euclid­ean, topol­o­gy-curved uni­verse — as we might plau­si­bly describe it today — laid out the basis for what would become math­e­mat­i­cal physics. In any case, the young Galileo’s lec­tures at the Flo­ren­tine Acad­e­my land­ed him a job as a math­e­mat­ics lec­tur­er at the Uni­ver­si­ty of Pisa, as good a rea­son as any for him to keep his pri­vate doubts to him­self. When it comes to sci­ence and reli­gion, as he must have known, you’ve got to pick your bat­tles.

Based in Seoul, Col­in Marshall writes and broad­casts on cities, lan­guage, and cul­ture. He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

title: Classical Musicians Interpret Astronauts' Footage of the Planet for Earth Music Theater
description: On the International Space Station (ISS), a module known as the Cupola allows astronauts to float into a small, window-filled viewing area. It’s u
body:
On the International Space Station (ISS), a module known as the Cupola allows astronauts to float into a small, window-filled viewing area. It’s used for observing high-tech exercises, spacewalks, and incoming vehicles, but it’s also a spectacular place to view what’s right outside: Earth.
Astronauts often take thousands of photos and videos of what they see from their lofty vantage point, and the Association of Space Explorers (ASE)—the professional association of astronauts who have flown on a mission, representing 43 countries—archives the footage for educational use. So far, the collection consists of more than seven million photos and movies. What to do with all of them? Enter Earth Music Theater.



Facilitated by ASE, Earth Music Theater is a multimedia project marrying sonic experiences with incredible imagery captured from above the earth. Musicians perform a combination of self-composed melodies and classical pieces, such as works by J.S. Bach. The video above, for example, features British Baroque ensemble Solomon’s Knot, while in several others, guitarist Steve Thomas interprets the footage through his own songs.
Imagery ranges from Jessica Meir’s capture of aurora australis moving across the earth’s atmosphere as the ISS orbits above Antarctica to remarkable shots of terrain and weather patterns. Earth Music Theater’s catalogue consists of dozens of movies, some of which are only a few minutes long and others that run the length of a feature film.
The initiative also occasionally coordinates live performances around the world, and you can also see recordings of these live performances on its website.

title: Lush Mixed-Media Collages by Clotilde Jiménez Piece Together an Artist's Lineage
description: Through vivid collages layering fragments of paper and fiber, Clotilde Jiménez echoes his own mélange of experiences and histories. The Mexico Cit
body:
Through vivid collages layering fragments of paper and fiber, Clotilde Jiménez echoes his own mélange of experiences and histories. The Mexico City-based artist was born in Honolulu to a Puerto Rican mother and African-American father, and he grew up in Philadelphia, before attending university in Cleveland and London. Both his heritage and ties to different cities around the globe nest together in his work, which draws references from the cultural and political contexts of each locale.
Using magazine clippings, Mexican craft paper, fabrics, and other pliable materials, Jiménez fashions dense portraits of his family alongside archetypal depictions of Blackness and masculinity. Fragments of burlap and thin woven strips add texture to “China de Mayagüez,” a vibrant autobiographical piece portraying a young Jiménez and his family member Juan. Rendered as a jíbaro, Juan evokes the subsistence farming traditions of Puerto Rico. Together, the pair pick oranges, while monarchs flutter among the fruits.
“Flower Portal 2” (2026). Photo by Ivo Loyola
The woven hat also appears in “The Nightcall,” worn by a woman enveloped in the blue light of darkness. Black birds with shiny plumage and blooming cacti flank the figure as a bouquet hangs from her hand. Fresh blooms also appear in the Flower Portal series, circular works that draw on Dutch still life paintings. Fish, faces, and beams of light augment lush bouquets, referencing both the fleeting nature of life and humble joys.
For this body of work, Jiménez dives into silences and what’s left unsaid in a family, particularly the secrets children aren’t privy to. In a recent conversation, he describes these pieces as visualizing a “revelation,” one that gave insight into a history of abuse. He explains: 

My grandmother, when I was an adult, randomly was like I need to tell you something, and she told me that my grandfather was not my real grandfather. It is actually his brother, the one who kind of looked out for you and raised you. Everything made sense. I’m not making excuses for abuse, but I’m seeing it a little bit more objectively now, why certain things were said, why certain things were done, why certain things were ignored. So the show is really about silence and how that forms us from a young age.

The collages shown here are included in the exhibition Éramos silencios, which translates to “we were silent,” on view through October 31 at Marianne Ibrahim’s Chicago gallery. Explore more of the artist’s work on Instagram.
“Invitation to the Altar” (2026). Photo by Alum Gálvez
“The Nightcall” (2025). Photo by Alum Gálvez
“Los Varones” (2026). Photo by Ivo Loyola
“Flower Portal 1” (2026). Photo by Ivo Loyola

title: France Celebrates the Bicentennial of Photography with Traveling Themed Exhibitions
description: In our era of digital screens and virtually endless images and videos, it’s a challenge to imagine the time before photography existed. Two centur
body:
In our era of digital screens and virtually endless images and videos, it’s a challenge to imagine the time before photography existed. Two centuries ago this year, French inventor Nicéphore Niépce successfully captured the first known permanent image. He called his new process héliographie, or “sun writing,” employing light-sensitive bitumen dissolved in lavender oil, which he used to coat a polished pewter plate.
After exposing the plate on his windowsill for several hours, an image of several outbuildings on Niépce’s property emerged, and photography as we know it was born. But it wasn’t until 1839, when Louis Jacques Mandé Daguerre announced his eponymous Daguerrotype, that photography entered the public realm. From there, variations in the chemistry and materials proliferated around the world, spurring advanced technologies and the phenomenon we continue to enjoy today, even in a digital form that feels worlds away from the first iterations.
Frédéric Boissonas, “Scène de danse rythmique à l’institut Jacques Dalcroze, 6 filles dansant.” © GrandPalaisRmn (Musée d’Orsay)/Hervé Lewandowski
Celebrating 200 years of photography in France, GrandPalaisRmn has organized a series of 11 themed, traveling exhibitions as part of the ambitious initiative titled Grand Angle. From 19th-century studio portraits and dance to rural life and the front lines of war, the shows highlight a wide range of subject matter and individuals behind the lens. The selections are drawn primarily from the vast archives of the GrandPalaisRmn and Médiathèque du patrimoine et de la photographie (MPP), which steward some 1.8 million digitized images altogether.
The shows are also coordinated in partnership with Centre national des arts plastiques (Cnap), the International Olympic Committee (IOC), and Fisheye, and they’re staged both around France and internationally. Ruralités, for example, just opened at the tourism office of Roubion, a small commune in southeastern France. And a solo exhibition of work by the late Willy Ronis is on view this month at the Châtel-Saint-Germain library. The program is slated to continue through September 2027.

Jacques Piarrat, “Danse 2.” © Paris Musées, Musée Carnavalet, courtesy of GrandPalaisRmn / Image Ville de Paris

title: German Duo Arrested After Hanging Paintings Next to Mona Lisa
description:
News
                The two men told Paris police the stunt was just "for fun."
body:
News
                The two men told Paris police the stunt was just "for fun."
            
                
                                
                            
                
                
                    Anna Lee
                    September 21, 2026
                            — 2 min read
                    
                
            
                
        
            Visitors observe Leonardo da Vinci's "Mona Lisa" at the Louvre. (photo Marc Piasecki/Getty Images)
    
        
            French authorities apprehended two German men at the Louvre Museum on Saturday, September 19, after they affixed two paintings to a wall in the room housing Leonardo da Vinci's “Mona Lisa.”Police told Agence France-Presse that the men used sticky tape to mount the 30 cm by 40 cm (~11.8 by 15.7 inches) paintings, one of which depicted one suspect in armor and the other showed the two with a woman. The duo reportedly told police that they completed the stunt “for fun.” Once the museum files a formal complaint, the men will be summoned to court and face charges for the minor damage done to the wall.While da Vinci's early 16th-century masterpiece reportedly sustained no damage during the stunt, the arrests come amid ongoing plans to move “Mona Lisa” to her own gallery. At her current station in the Salle des États exhibition hall, “Mona Lisa” is surrounded by paintings that receive comparably little attention, such as Paolo Veronese’s “The Wedding Feast at Cana” (1562–63).

title: Naomi Beckwith Says She's "Not Afraid" of Pro-Palestine Protest at Documenta 16
description:
News
                “People have a right to protest and express their opinions,” the curator told Die Zeit, revealing that some
body:
News
                “People have a right to protest and express their opinions,” the curator told Die Zeit, revealing that some artists have declined to participate in the exhibition over “Germany's position on the Gaza war.”
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Documenta 16 Artistic Director Naomi Beckwith in June 2025 (photo Swen Pförtner/picture alliance via Getty Images)
    
        
            With less than a year until Documenta 16 opens in Kassel, Germany, artistic director Naomi Beckwith said in a recent interview that some artists declined to participate in the exhibition over “Germany's position on the Gaza war” and concerns about artistic freedom in the country.Speaking to the German newspaper Die Zeit, Beckwith declined to answer directly when asked about her personal stance on Gaza, stating that the more important question was “how we can overcome this divisive mindset,” and “how can we start talking to one another again?”“I understand the need for solidarity and support, but we’re not going to get anywhere with entrenched sides,” Beckwith explained when prompted. Early last year, the exhibition's organization adopted the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance's (IHRA) working definition of antisemitism, which is widely criticized for its conflation of anti-Zionism with antisemitism. Documenta incorporated IHRA's definition after its particularly controversial 15th edition in 2022, curated by the Indonesian art collective ruangrupa. The collective and several other advisors and artist participants — including Palestinian collective The Question of Funding — were accused of antisemitism in a fringe Zionist blog post that was cited by various German media outlets reporting on the matter ahead of the exhibition's opening. A view of Indonesian collective Taring Padi’s People’s Justice installation assembled at Documenta 15 before its subsequent removal (photo Hakan Topal/Hyperallergic)
